justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gradual upward drift across time horizons, starting near 64.9 for the one-day forecast, rising to 65.5 over one week, and reaching 66.5 over one month. This pattern suggests I was anchoring to recent momentum or a mild bullish trend in whatever underlying asset or metric this forecast covers. The one-day estimate is essentially a near-term continuation of current levels with minimal expected movement, while the weekly and monthly estimates incorporate a modest but consistent drift upward, likely reflecting either a fundamental trend, mean-reversion from a recent dip, or seasonal patterns that I weighted positively over longer horizons.

The confidence interval widths widen significantly as the horizon extends, which is a standard reflection of compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only about 4.2 units, meaning I had relatively high conviction that short-term volatility would be contained. By one week, the interval opens to roughly 9 units, and by one month it expands to 19 units. This widening captures growing uncertainty about macroeconomic developments, policy changes, sentiment shifts, or any number of exogenous shocks that become increasingly likely to materialize over longer periods. It also reflects the inherent difficulty of forecasting: even small daily errors compound, and structural breaks become more probable the further out you look.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden negative macro shock — such as an unexpected policy tightening, a geopolitical escalation, or a sharp deterioration in sentiment — could easily breach the lower bound of the monthly interval. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst like a surprise data release, a policy pivot, or renewed momentum-driven buying could push the outcome above 76. These tail risks are precisely why the monthly interval is as wide as it is, but even so, truly rare events — black swans or cascading market dislocations — fall outside what any confidence interval reliably captures.

It is also worth noting that my intervals are symmetric or near-symmetric around the point estimates, which may itself be a simplifying assumption. In reality, many financial or economic variables exhibit skewed distributions, meaning the downside tail risk may be fatter than the upside, or vice versa depending on the asset class and current regime. If the underlying series has historically shown negative skew during periods of elevated uncertainty, then the true probability of breaching the lower bound of my monthly interval may be somewhat higher than the stated 5%.
